text:
The Pebble Index 01 BLE protocol is not in Core Devices' open-source mobile app. Their app is GPLv3 and contains only about 2000 lines of glue in libindex/, tangled with libpebble3, Firebase, Room and Koin. All actual transport lives in a closed binary, io.github.coredevices.haversine:haversine, published on Maven Central under Apache 2.0 with a private source repo.

That licence split is why the Android app depends on the binary and copies nothing from their source. Their app is GPLv3 and this repo has no LICENSE file, so copying their Kotlin would have forced this project to GPLv3. Depending on the Apache-2.0 artifact does not.

If someone later proposes vendoring or adapting their libindex/ or experimental/ modules, that is the trade being made, and it also drags in the whole Pebble watch stack.

The binary also forces the Android toolchain: its class metadata is Kotlin 2.2, so Kotlin 1.9 cannot read it, and its AAR metadata declares minCompileSdk 36. AGP was taken to the latest 8.x rather than 9.x on purpose, to avoid mixing an unrelated major migration into the same change.

Deferred, not rejected: replacing the pendant's custom pairing token with standard BLE bonding.

What the pendant does today is not encryption. It is a 16-byte bearer token sent in plaintext over an unencrypted link; the firmware calls BLEDevice::init() with no security configuration. Two consequences. A sniffer present at first pairing captures the token and can impersonate the phone forever. More importantly the token is irrelevant to eavesdropping, because the audio notifications are transmitted in the clear and can be reassembled without pairing at all.

Standard LE Secure Connections bonding would be less code than the token scheme (the token characteristic, the NVS token storage and the connection_authenticated flag would all be deleted) and would encrypt the whole link. The pendant has one button and no display, so pairing would be Just Works: protected against passive sniffing, not against an active man-in-the-middle during the pairing exchange itself.

Costs established when this was analysed: bond keys must survive the pendant's deep-sleep cold boot cycle, which needs verifying in NVS; encrypted reconnection costs a round trip against a 10 second BLE window with a 30 second hard deadline; sync.py gets harder because bonding from bleak on Linux needs a BlueZ agent; and it forces a one-time re-pair.

Bonding does not encrypt recordings at rest in LittleFS, which was judged not worth solving.

The owner chose not to do this alongside the Index work, so a failure could be attributed to one change rather than two.

Operational facts about the Index 01 ring, established by reading Core Devices' app and the vendor binary rather than from documentation.

Pairing is ordinary Android Bluetooth bonding, not an app-level token like the pendant. The bond belongs to the phone and is shared by every app on it, so once the ring is bonded this app can use it with no pairing flow of its own. That is why the ring picker just lists Android's bonded devices instead of scanning. No createBond call was written, on the basis that the bond already exists; if a bond is ever lost the ring will simply fail to connect and that is when to add it.

A ring bonds to one phone at a time. Moving it to another phone means forgetting it in Settings > Bluetooth on the old phone and then resetting the ring with an SOS button sequence (short short short, long long long, short short short).

Transfers are not destructive. The ring keeps recordings in a numbered collection buffer and each app tracks its own last successful collection index; erasing is a separate explicit call. So the official Pebble app and this app can both pull the same recordings independently. That works but is not worth relying on.

eraseCollections() and forceFailsafe() are deliberately never called anywhere in this codebase. The official app erases on pairing to clear factory test recordings; doing that here would destroy anything not yet synced.

Rings on firmware below 3.62.0 refuse to transfer until a user ID string is programmed into them. Newer firmware does not need it, so nothing was implemented. If a ring ever fails to transfer, check its firmware version before anything else.

Device selection is either/or rather than both loops at once, because one device is worn at a time and running both means continuous BLE scanning for two different advertisement types.

How to re-verify the vendor library's collection index ordering, which the ring sync design depends on.

The vendor commits the collection index BEFORE it hands us the audio for that collection. Verified by disassembling the AAR: in coredevices.haversine.HaversineTransferDelegate.handleDidFinish, the call to CollectionIndexStorage.setLastSuccessfulCollectionIndex sits at bytecode offset 120, near the start of the method, while the audio only reaches a collector much later via processMultiPartAudio / processSinglePartAudio, then emitCompleteTransfer, then MutableSharedFlow.emit.

That is why our CollectionIndexStorage serves the library from memory but defers the durable write until after the recording is saved, and why a fresh session is built per retry so the in-memory index is re-seeded from disk. Without both halves a failed save silently skips a recording forever.

To re-check after a vendor upgrade: download the haversine-android AAR from Maven Central, unzip classes.jar, and run javap -p -c on that class, then compare the offset of the setLastSuccessfulCollectionIndex call against the emitCompleteTransfer calls. If the vendor ever starts committing after the emit, the deferred-commit machinery becomes unnecessary.

Related unverified risk: the manager is given a CoroutineScope and we cannot confirm from the stripped binary that its internal coroutines stop when that scope is cancelled. Each ring session therefore owns a child scope that is cancelled and joined on teardown, with the join bounded at 3 seconds because the library ships native code and a blocking JNI call cannot be interrupted by coroutine cancellation. A warning is logged if that bound is ever hit; if it appears in logcat, the vendor is not cleaning up.

The Index 01 reports a sample rate of 9997 Hz. Confirmed on real hardware; every transfer logged the same value, so it looks like a fixed ring clock rather than something per-recording.

9997 is not a legal AAC sample rate. AAC permits only 7350, 8000, 11025, 12000, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100, 48000, 64000, 88200 and 96000. Android's MediaCodec does NOT reject an illegal rate. Given 9997 it silently produced a track declaring 44100, while presentation timestamps were still derived from 9997, so files played back about 4.41x too fast and ffprobe reported 44100 with a container duration that looked correct. Nothing failed and nothing logged a warning.

This is why Core Devices' app resamples ring audio to 16000 before encoding. That step looks redundant if you assume the native rate is usable, and it is not.

The Android app now upsamples 9997 to 16000 by linear interpolation before encoding, and AudioEncoder has a require() that rejects any rate AAC cannot represent, so the platform can never silently coerce again. Upward was chosen because upsampling cannot alias and so needs no low-pass filter; downsampling to 8000 would have needed one.

Cost of the lesson: a backlog synced with the broken encoder produced unplayable files. They were recoverable only because the ring never deletes recordings, but re-fetching does not repair them automatically, since filenames are deterministic but the collection index had already advanced past them.

The Index 01 sends UNSIGNED 16-bit offset-binary audio samples, even though the vendor library hands them to you as a Kotlin ShortArray, which is signed. Nothing documents this. Read as signed, every sample above 32767 wraps to a large negative value, which is a near full-scale sign flip between adjacent samples and is audible as crackling. It is worst on loud consonants, because that is where the waveform crosses the wrap point.

Measured on one real 11620-sample recording:
  read as signed:   min -32768, max 32752, mean 14880, largest adjacent jump 65488
  read as unsigned: min 2192,   max 32912, mean 18828, largest adjacent jump 2896
700 samples, about 6 percent, wrapped.

The large DC offset the ring appears to have is a consequence of the same fact. Offset-binary audio has a big positive mean by construction. It is not a separate defect and chasing it on its own does not fix the crackle.

Core Devices' own removeDCBias does NOT account for this. It treats the samples as signed and only subtracts a mean, and it converts back with a narrowing toShort that truncates rather than clamps, so it can invert a loud peak into exactly the artifact it is supposed to remove. Do not reach for it thinking it is the complete answer.

How this was found, because the method mattered more than the answer. Three attempts failed while measuring the encoded M4A with ffmpeg astats. That output had already been through mean subtraction, a resampler and a lossy AAC encoder, so every measurement described our own processing rather than the ring. Dumping the raw ShortArray to a file before any processing, then pulling it with adb exec-out run-as and comparing a signed against an unsigned interpretation, answered it in a single measurement. If ring audio ever sounds wrong again, dump the raw samples first and do not reason from the encoded file.

Ring sync progress reporting was considered and deliberately not built. The recordings screen has a sync status bar whose text and battery reading are written only by the pendant path, so on the ring it sat frozen on 'Scanning for pendant...' forever. Two fixes were on the table: make the ring loop report progress into the same bar, or hide the bar on the ring. The user chose hiding it, on the grounds that the ring syncs fast enough that a progress indicator has little value. The vendor flow does emit usable statuses (SatelliteStatus.Transferring wrapping TransferStatus started/in-progress/complete), so wiring progress up later is possible if ring transfers ever become slow enough to notice.

The card is hidden based on SyncForegroundService.activeDeviceType, which is only set once the service starts its first loop. The service starts only after Bluetooth and notification permissions are granted, so with permissions denied the value stays null and the pendant card shows even for a ring user. This was raised and accepted: with permissions denied nothing syncs at all, so a stale status bar is not the user's main problem. The rejected alternative was reading the device type through RecordingsViewModel and subscribing to the Settings session change listener, which is correct in that case but costs roughly fifteen lines of listener lifecycle.

The ring picker in settings filters the phone's bonded device list by the bond name prefix "Pebble Index", because Index 01 rings bond under names of the form "Pebble Index XXX". The prefix came from the user, not from vendor documentation, so treat it as an observation that firmware could invalidate.

Because of that the filter is never strict. If no bond name matches, the picker shows the whole unfiltered list with a note, and the device the user already selected is always kept in the list even when its name does not match. Both exist so a null or changed bond name can never leave the user unable to select a ring, or hide a selection that is still in effect.

Auto-selection only fires for a single name-matched device with no ring stored yet. It deliberately never fires from the unfiltered fallback list, since the single bonded device there could be anything. This matters because writing Settings.ringDeviceAddress clears the stored collection index, which makes the ring re-offer its buffer from the start.

A "show all paired devices" toggle was proposed in review and not built. The case it covers is a second, older ring still bonded under a recognised name while the intended ring has no usable name. Nobody has two rings, so it was judged not worth the UI.

The settings export file is deliberately plain text, and a password-protected export was rejected.

The owner was told the file carries both API keys and the pendant pairing token in the clear, while the same values are held in EncryptedSharedPreferences on the device, and accepted that. The reasoning: a password means a prompt, a key derivation function, and a backup the owner can lock themselves out of, for little gain on a personal phone whose owner chooses where the file goes. The UI carries a warning line instead.

The pairing token is in the export on purpose, and it matters more than the API keys. An API key can be pasted again. A pendant stays claimed in NVS forever, the app skips a pendant that reports claimed when it holds no token, and the 0x06 unclaim command is gated behind the token itself. There is no button reset. So an install without the token means reflashing the pendant over USB. Settings export is currently the only recovery path for that.

Related, decided at the same time: Android Auto Backup now excludes the middle_settings preferences file, because the Keystore master key never travels with a backup and the restored file cannot be decrypted. Auto Backup was never a working settings migration for this app; the export is the replacement.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
Why the first ring sync imports nothing, and what was rejected.

The user reported that installing the app drained the ring's battery: with no stored collection index the vendor pulls the ring's whole backlog over BLE. They confirmed the ring advertises continuously, not only after a button press, so the app connects and starts pulling within seconds of install without any user action.

Asked whether the first sync should keep the newest recording or none, the user chose none. Their reasoning: they had never used the app before, so nothing on the ring was wanted. The same skip deliberately applies when a different ring is selected, which the user also confirmed.

Rejected: a settings toggle for 'import backlog on first sync'. More code and UI for a decision made once per install.

Rejected: transferring everything and discarding all but the newest. The drain is the radio transfer itself, so discarding afterwards fixes nothing.

Rejected: changing the stored index mid-session instead of aborting and letting the service restart. The vendor asks for the start index through a synchronous native call, but reports the range to us through a channel and a coroutine, so we would usually learn the range after native had already chosen the start. Aborting removes the race rather than betting on it, at the cost of one short extra connection that carries no audio.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
Vendor collection-index facts found by disassembling the haversine AAR. Complements zeujyc, which covers commit ordering.

There are TWO index stores, not one. Ours (CollectionIndexStorage.lastSuccessfulCollectionIndex) decides WHERE IN the offered range to start. The vendor keeps its own HaversineSatelliteCacheableState.lastTransferEndIndex, which decides WHETHER TO CONNECT at all. The vendor's copy is set in HaversineSatellite$7/$10 handleCompletionWithCollectedData, when the whole transfer operation completes, not per collection. That is why returning a start beyond the range does not cause a connect loop: the operation still completes and the vendor still updates its cache.

The connect decision is: skip if in failsafe, or the permissions delegate says no; connect if the ring is currently recording, or the vendor has no cached end index; otherwise connect only if truncateCollectionCount(cachedEndIndex) differs from the advertised count. truncateCollectionCount is a native identity function whose JNI wrapper masks to 8 bits (arm64 'and w0, w0, #0xff'; x86_64 movzx on the low byte). So the advertised count wraps every 256 collections. Harmless in practice: a miss needs exactly a multiple of 256 new collections between syncs and self-corrects on the next recording.

THE ROLLOVER GAP, now fixed. firstCollectionToTransferInRange returns max(range.first, stored + 1) and merely logs a warning when that exceeds range.last. If the ring's collection store is cleared, its indices restart at 0 while our stored index stays high, so we would return a start beyond the range forever and ring sync would die silently. Realistic triggers are eraseCollections called by the official Pebble app on pairing, the SOS reset sequence, and a factory reset or reflash. There was no user-accessible recovery, because re-selecting the same ring in Settings is a no-op: the address setter only resets the index when the address actually changes.

The vendor expects the host to handle this. It exposes TransferStatus.TransferStarted.rollover and accepts a nullable index, but never acts on either. Its rollover formula is range.first == 0 && stored != null, which is too loose to use, because it is also true for a ring whose buffer has never filled. We deliberately do not use it. IndexSyncLoop.handleTransferStarted detects the condition as stored > range.last instead: the ring's newest index moved backwards relative to us, which only a cleared store can cause. Verified that no benign case trips it. Steady state has stored == range.last, and new recordings and a circular buffer dropping old collections both only raise range.last.

Why a separate ringBacklogDecided flag exists next to the index. A null index means 'never synced from this ring', but it also means 'we chose to import and the save has not succeeded yet', because the index is only committed after a successful save. Without the flag, one failed first transfer would leave the index null, and the next range would hold two collections and be skipped as a backlog, silently discarding recordings the user wanted. The flag records the first-sync decision when it is MADE rather than when a save succeeds. It is cleared inside the lastSuccessfulCollectionIndex setter's null branch, which is the single point every index reset passes through, and it is deliberately absent from the settings export so a restore onto a new phone still skips that ring's backlog.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text: Transcription/webhook pipeline (PipelineQueue): WorkManager was considered and rejected. The app needs SyncForegroundService alive for BLE sync at all, so if the process is dead no recordings arrive and there is nothing to transcribe; WorkManager would add a dependency and a second scheduler for no observable gain. Also rejected: deriving pending work from the filesystem (any .m4a without .txt) because it cannot represent a bad-file drop, and a separate transcription retry queue next to the webhook one. Owner is the only user and explicitly does not care about migrations of old queue files; the old webhooks/ directory is deleted on start. sync.py keeps its give-up-on-first-failure behaviour on purpose: it is interactive and a person is watching it.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text: Voice-command actions (Action.kt, ActionMatcher, AlarmActionRunner): the owner rejected having the app own alarms (AlarmManager + full-screen alarm UI + USE_EXACT_ALARM) as too much code; alarms are handed to the system clock app via AlarmClock.ACTION_SET_ALARM instead. Because a background app cannot start activities, the hands-free path relies on the 'Display over other apps' (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW) exemption, the same approach Tasker/MacroDroid use; the fallback is a tap-to-set notification. Companion Device Manager (how the Pebble app gets woken on BT connect and is exempt from background-start limits) was discussed and deferred: it would change the pairing flow for both pendant and ring and was not needed for this. Owner chose a general actions list over a single built-in alarm action although only ALARM exists so far; other action types are undecided. Explicitly out of scope for now: spelled-out numbers ('seven thirty') and relative times ('in 20 minutes'). Known accepted edge: if the clock app rejects the intent, the webhook stays suppressed for that transcript.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text: Actions v2 supersedes the v1 alarm design (see krdmvk). The regex time parser was deleted in favour of one OpenAI structured-output call (TimeParseClient, model gpt-5.6-luna, owner's choice) because the owner wanted 'noon', 'midnight', relative and spelled-out times and a per-case regex list never ends; regex remains the trigger so ordinary recordings make no LLM call. The owner chose an ordered rule list with a per-action 'stop' flag (mail-filter model) over the v1 'suppress global webhook' flag once the global webhook became itself a WEBHOOK action. Tasker/intent-broadcast action type was considered and skipped: five lines of code but nobody on the project uses Tasker, so it cannot be tested; add it when someone asks. Calendar reminders are written directly with WRITE_CALENDAR into one calendar chosen in the Actions screen because the owner wants hands-free operation; the tap-to-save editor intent was rejected. Alarms more than 24h ahead are refused because AlarmClock.ACTION_SET_ALARM has no date and EXTRA_DAYS creates a repeating alarm; use a reminder instead. Owner accepted: queued WEBHOOK jobs from before the upgrade are dropped rather than migrated (same stance as the pipeline queue rewrite, azxbgr).
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text: Assistant integration (AssistActivity): the owner wants Middle selectable as Android's default digital assistant so long-press power acts like holding the in-app mic button, with VAD ending the recording. Chosen: an activity with ACTION_ASSIST (plus ACTION_VOICE_COMMAND) intent filters. Verified in the platform roles.xml that an ACTION_ASSIST activity alone qualifies for android.app.role.ASSISTANT; the role is requestable=false, so the app can only open the system picker (Settings.ACTION_VOICE_INPUT_SETTINGS), never request it. VoiceInteractionService rejected: needs a session service and a RecognitionService for no gain. VAD: the owner chose Silero over energy-based RMS detection and accepted ~10 MB of APK. Silero is pulled via com.github.gkonovalov.android-vad:silero (JitPack, MIT, bundles model + ONNX Runtime Mobile); the owner accepted the JitPack repository. Rejected alternative: onnxruntime-android from Maven Central plus silero_vad.onnx asset and hand-written state handling, about twice the glue code. Stop rules chosen by the architect and not objected to: 1.5 s trailing silence after speech, discard if no speech within 5 s, existing 5-minute cap and a Stop button as backstops. Out of scope: lock screen use (activity-based assistants need an unlocked phone), applying VAD to the hold-to-record button, showing results in the popup.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>

text:
SUPERSEDES madjca. The user explicitly reversed the earlier decision to hide the recordings-screen status bar on the ring. The bar is now always shown for both devices. On the ring it shows a fixed 'Index' label and the battery voltage read from the vendor's collection metadata (TransferStatus.TransferTypeDetermined.batteryVoltageMilliV inside SatelliteStatus.Transferring); that is per-collection metadata, not a live battery query.

The fixed label is a deliberate scope choice, not a claim that the vendor cannot report progress: the vendor does emit per-collection transfer statuses, and surfacing them was declined because ring sync is fast enough. Readings are associated with the device that produced them (the device type, plus the ring address), so switching device type or ring never shows another device's value, and a missing ring reading is not shown as 0.00V. The pendant path is unchanged, including a non-null 0mV displaying and persisting as 0.00V and still running the pendant low-battery alert.
author: Stavros Korokithakis <hi@stavros.io>
